title: Your true worth
summary: Where my sense of worth comes from and who has the right to tell me who I am. Despite childhood wounds, comparisons and a sense of inferiority, God calls me his child, made on purpose, treasured and accepted in Christ.

sections.heading: Where do I get the answer to "who am I"?

items.comment: The first word about my worth does not belong to me or to the people who hurt me - it belongs to the One who "knit me together." I exist on purpose, not by accident.

questions.text: Whose voices have most shaped what you think about yourself today? What would change if God had the last word?

items.label: Ps 139 as a foundation of dignity, not surveillance
items.content: Psalm 139 links God's all-knowing and all-present nature with the act of creation ("you knit me together," v. 13). When it comes to identity, the key point is that the God who knows me to the depths also treasures me - being fully known and being accepted go together. This is the opposite of the fear that "if anyone really knew me, they would reject me."

questions.text: What are you most afraid God will "see" in you? How does this fear change in light of the fact that he sees everything - and still says "precious"?

items.label: "you knit me together" / סָכַךְ (sakak) (Ps 139:13)
items.content: The Hebrew verb used in v. 13 (usually translated "knit" or "wove") carries the image of careful, hands-on weaving - like a weaver at the loom. My existence is not the result of a random process but the attentive work of the Creator. This is the biblical foundation of a dignity that comes before any achievement or appearance of mine.

items.comment: God calls me by name and says "you are mine." My identity is neither anonymous nor accidental - it rests on the fact that someone knows me and chooses me.

questions.text: What do you feel when you hear God speak your name and the words "you are mine" - before you achieve anything?

items.comment: "You are precious in my eyes, and honored." God's valuation of a person does not depend on their usefulness or success - it is a decision of love.

questions.text: How is being "useful" different from being "precious"? What do you base your daily sense of worth on?

items.label: God as Redeemer / גָּאַל (ga'al) (Iz 43,1)
items.content: Just before the words "you are mine" (v. 1), God presents himself as the One who "redeemed you." The Hebrew *ga'al* is the action of the "kinsman-redeemer" (go'el), who would buy back a family member out of slavery or debt. So my worth is not merely declared - it is backed by action: God himself steps into the role of a close relative in order to win me back.

questions.text: What changes in your sense of worth when you realize that God not only says "you are precious" but actually "buys you back" like a close relative?

sections.heading: The wound of inferiority and comparison

items.comment: People look at what is visible; God looks at the heart. Many wounds of inferiority come from measuring ourselves by someone else's standard - looks, status, opinion.

questions.text: By what "standard" do you most often judge yourself? What would change if you accepted God's standard?

items.label: the image of God as dignity that cannot be undone (Rdz 1,26-27)
items.content: It is worth stressing that humanity was placed at the summit of creation as the "image of God," deliberately designed ("Let us make man") and not a random product. That is why an attack on human life is treated as an attack on God himself, whom that person represents (Gen 9:6). Since dignity flows from being God's image, it cannot be "earned" or "lost" through someone else's judgment.

questions.text: If your dignity is built into the fact that you are God's image, whose opinion actually has the right to undo it?

items.comment: Paul urges us to test our own work rather than compare ourselves with others. Comparison always drives us either into pride or into a sense of inferiority - never into the truth.

questions.text: Who do you compare yourself with most often, and what does it do to you? What would a life free of that comparison look like?

items.comment: "Though my father and mother forsake me, the Lord will take me in." For those wounded in childhood, this is a promise that an early rejection is not the last word.

questions.text: Which early experience most strongly told you that you are "not enough"? How does this verse answer it?

sections.heading: A new name: a child of God

items.comment: To those who receive Jesus, he gives the right to become children of God. The identity of a child is a gift to receive, not a reward to win.

questions.text: How is trying to "earn" acceptance different from receiving it as a gift?

items.comment: "See what love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God - and that is what we are." This is not a metaphor but a new status.

questions.text: What changes in your daily thinking about yourself when you take the sentence "I am a child of God" seriously and repeat it?

items.label: "children of God" / τέκνα θεοῦ (tekna theou) (J 1,12; 1 J 3,1)
items.content: John uses the word *tekna* ("children," "those born"), emphasizing a real birth from God and not merely the legal status of adoption. The Christian's identity therefore rests on a new origin - from God (cf. John 1:13), which makes it independent of human lineage, achievements or the opinions of others.

questions.text: If my deepest identity comes from being "born of God," what loses its power over my sense of worth?

items.label: "See!" / ἴδετε (idete) as a call to wonder (1 J 3,1)
items.content: John opens the verse with the imperative *idete* - "look!", "see for yourselves!" This is not a cool statement of status but an invitation to stop and marvel at the scale of the love that makes us children. A healthy identity is born not from analyzing ourselves but from gazing at the Father's love.

items.comment: We are children of God "through faith in Christ" - not through lineage, achievements or being flawless. Entry into the family is equal for everyone.

questions.text: If everyone enters God's family by the same road of faith, what does that say about your place in it?

items.comment: We have received "the Spirit of adoption," in whom we cry out "Abba, Father." The Spirit himself testifies to our spirit that we are children - this is not auto-suggestion.

questions.text: What would it mean to relate to God as a loving "Dad" rather than as a distant judge?

items.label: "adoption as sons" / υἱοθεσία (hyiothesia) (Rz 8,15; Ef 1,5)
items.content: Paul reaches for the term *hyiothesia* - adoption from the world of Roman law. An adopted son received the full rights of an heir, and his former debts lost their force. This is a picture of an identity received as a gift: I am not "promoted" to child status by my merits but brought into the family by the Father's decision, with full rights of inheritance.

questions.text: What changes in your picture of God when you see that the status of a child is a legal act of the Father, not a reward for your "performance"?

items.label: "Abba" as the language of closeness (Rz 8,15)
items.content: *Abba* is the everyday Aramaic word a child in the family used to address their father - close to our "daddy." Paul leaves it untranslated because it carries a tenderness that the Greek *pater* did not fully convey. The Spirit puts on our lips not a title of distance but a word of trusting, family closeness.

items.comment: The prodigal son wants to come back on the terms of a hired servant; the father restores him as a son - robe, ring, feast. God does not accept us "halfway"; he restores our dignity in full.

questions.text: Where are you trying to come back to God "as a hired servant"? What would it mean to let him restore you to full sonship?

items.comment: God chose us "before the foundation of the world" and destined us for adoption as his children. My worth has the deepest foundation - a decision God made before I existed.

questions.text: What does it give you to know that God "had you in mind" and chose you before you could do anything or ruin anything?

items.comment: We are "graced in the Beloved"; we have redemption and forgiveness. Identity in Christ also includes the fact that guilt no longer defines who I am.

questions.text: What shapes your self-image more - your failures, or the fact that you are "accepted in the Beloved"?

items.label: "in the Beloved" / ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ (en to egapemeno) (Ef 1,6)
items.content: Paul does not say we are graced "for our merits" but "in the Beloved" - my identity is immersed in the One whom the Father loves perfectly. The participle *egapemenos* (literally "the One who is loved") is a title of Christ; being "in him," I enter the circle of that same love. The point of reference is no longer comparison with others but belonging to the Beloved.

questions.text: How is the thought "I am accepted when I earn it" different from "I am accepted because I am in the Beloved"?

items.label: redemption at a price / ἀπολύτρωσις (apolytrosis) (Ef 1,7)
items.content: The word *apolytrosis* meant the ransom of a slave or captive for a set price. The verse links it directly with the "blood" of Christ - so my worth is measured by the price God was willing to pay. It is worth stressing that the worth God assigns to a person should fill us with grateful joy; it does not come from our achievements but from the act of redemption.

items.comment: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation." The past does not vanish from memory, but it stops being the definition of who I am.

questions.text: What in your past is hardest for you to accept as "what has passed"? How does the word about a new creation speak to it?

items.label: a "new name" as identity given by God (Ap 2,17)
items.content: In Revelation the one who overcomes receives "a white stone, and on it a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it." In the ancient world a name expressed a person's essence and destiny. God reserves for himself the right to give me a new name - it is he, not my wounds or the labels from my past, who has the last word on who I really am.

questions.text: What "name" (label) do you quietly carry about yourself? What would it mean to let God give you a new one?

items.comment: "A chosen people, a royal priesthood, a people for God's own possession" - an identity that is not an individual achievement but belonging to a community chosen by God.

questions.text: How does it change your sense of worth to know that you belong to something greater than yourself - to the people of God?

application.text: Your worth is not the rating people give you, your successes, or the wounds of your past. God made you on purpose, knows you to the depths and calls you "precious," and in Jesus he makes you his child - chosen, accepted, new. You do not have to earn it; you can receive it. A healthy sense of worth is born not from comparisons but from the certainty of whose you are.
application.challenge: Write down 3-4 sentences you usually use to describe yourself (e.g. "I am worthless," "I am not enough"). Next to each one, write a single sentence God speaks about you from this study (e.g. 1 John 3:1; Isa 43:4; Eph 1:6) together with the reference. For a week, read these words of God aloud every day - and tell God plainly which one is hardest for you to receive.
